title: The Hedgehog Choir's Jumbled Song
markdown:
Once upon a time, in a garden that smelled like warm sunshine and sweet flowers, lived a little hedgehog named Ivy. Ivy had the cheeriest prickles you ever did see, like little brown buttons all over her back. And when Ivy was happy, her voice was clear and bright. It sounded like a little bluebell in the morning sun. Ivy was part of the Sunny Meadow Hedgehog Choir. And oh, how they loved to sing.

The Grand Meadow Fair was coming soon. It was the biggest party of the year, with bright stalls and yummy treats. The hedgehog choir had been practising their best song, called The Sunbeam Song, for a very, very long time. They practised under the big shady oak tree. They practised by the gurgling brook, where the water sang its own happy tune. And they practised right here, in Old Tom’s cozy garden.

Old Tom, the gardener, was their leader. His cheeks were as rosy as ripe apples, and he always had his big green watering can near. He wore a straw hat that was a little too big, which made him look quite funny and very kind. He’d tap his little silver trowel to help his spiky singers keep time. Tap-tap-tap went the trowel.

“Alright, my little spiky singers,” Old Tom would call out, his voice warm and steady. “Let’s sing from the part about the butterflies dancing. Ready now?”

And with a rustle of prickles, they would begin. “Flutter, flutter, on the breeze,” sang the hedgehogs, their voices full of sunshine. But each little hedgehog liked to sing at their own special speed. Little Pip, who was always in a super-duper hurry, would sing very, very fast. “Flutterflutterflutter onthebreeze,” he’d sing, a tiny speedy blur. Then there was Bertha, who liked to sing her notes very slowly, like she was tasting sweet honey. She’d sing, “Flllluuuuuuttteeeeerrrr… onnnn… theeee… breeeeeeze…” so slowly, the butterflies might have taken a nap and woken up again before she was done.

Ivy tried her very, very best to keep up. She’d wiggle her nose and puff out her chest, trying to go fast like Pip, then slow down for Bertha. Rory the raccoon, who loved to join in, would add a cheerful chitter-chatter-chitter to the songs. But the song sounded like a jumble of happy noises. It was like a whole bunch of clocks all ticking at different times.

Old Tom would scratch his head, his straw hat wobbling. His trowel would tap a confused rhythm on his knee. “Oh dear, oh me. This Sunbeam Song sounds more like a Sunbeam Scramble.” He didn’t get cross, not Old Tom. He just looked very thoughtful, his eyes twinkling with a gentle wonder.

Rory the raccoon giggled, his furry tail swishing happily. “It sounds like we’re all singing different songs at once, Old Tom. Like a whole zoo of singers.”

Ivy felt a little bit sad. She had wanted their song to be just perfect for the Grand Meadow Fair. “We’re trying our best, Old Tom,” she said softly, her little nose twitching.

Old Tom looked at his choir. He saw Pip singing like a little rocket. He saw Bertha singing like a slow sleepy cloud. And he saw all the other hedgehogs in between, singing with all their might, each in their own special way. Then a wonderful bright twinkle appeared in his kind eyes. “Ah. Perhaps we don’t need to sing it all at the same speed.”

The hedgehogs blinked their little eyes. “Different speeds?” chirped Ivy, her sadness floating away like a dandelion seed.

“Indeed,” Old Tom declared, tapping his trowel with a happy little thump-thump-thump. “What if Pip sings his speedy flutter, and Bertha sings her slow lovely sway, and all of you in the middle sing your own beautiful pace? We’ll weave them all together. We’ll call it The Sunbeam Symphony of Speeds.”

And so Old Tom began to change the song. He gave Pip the very beginning, a fast and cheerful burst of notes, like a quick hello. Then, as Pip’s speedy notes gently faded, Bertha would begin her slow drawn-out melody, like a long warm hug. The other hedgehogs would join in their own perfect time, creating layers and layers of delightful sound. It wasn’t neat and tidy like a single straight river. It was more like a vibrant field of wildflowers, each bloom wonderfully beautiful and unique.

Soon it was the day of the Grand Meadow Fair. The hedgehog choir stood on the little wooden stage. The sun was shining, and so were their faces. Ivy took a deep breath, her heart feeling light and fluttery. Pip began, a flash of bright quick notes. Then Bertha, a gentle drawn-out hum that seemed to make time itself slow down. Soon all the hedgehogs were singing, their voices weaving together like colourful ribbons in the wind, each at its own delightful speed. The audience of squirrels, rabbits, and even a few wise old owls clapped and cheered with all their might.

They didn’t win a prize for being the most in-tune. They won a special prize for being the most unique and joyful. Ivy’s heart felt as light as a fluffy feather. Rory chittered with glee, and even Bertha, who was usually so slow, slowed down just long enough to give Ivy a happy little nuzzle of her soft nose.

Old Tom smiled, his straw hat tilted just so. He watched the happy faces in the audience. The watering can sat by the stage like a quiet extra singer. The Sunbeam Song had not gone straight, and the garden smelled, still, of warm sunshine and sweet flowers.
characters: Ivy (bluebell-voice hedgehog), Rory (choir-joining raccoon), Old Tom (rosy-cheek gardener)
